title: Watch Soviet Animations of Winnie the Pooh, Created by the Innovative Animator Fyodor Khitruk
description:
in Animation |   	November 3rd, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			
In 1962, the ani­ma­tor Fyo­dor Khitruk made his direc­to­r­i­al debut with Sto­ry of On
body:
in Animation |   	November 3rd, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			
In 1962, the ani­ma­tor Fyo­dor Khitruk made his direc­to­r­i­al debut with Sto­ry of One Crime, a film that broke with a Sovi­et ten­den­cy to make imi­ta­tions of Dis­ney-style ani­ma­tions. The film, as The Guardian explained in its 2012 obit­u­ary for the ani­ma­tor, came as a shock. It was styl­is­ti­cal­ly sim­ple and dealt with themes that Dis­ney films would nev­er touch — like, why would a polite clerk mur­der two house­wives with a fry­ing pan?
Khitruk made oth­er films that were packed with social com­men­tary, often tak­ing aim at abus­es in the Sovi­et sys­tem. But, he also made straight­for­ward ani­ma­tions for chil­dren, none more famous than his series of films based on AA Mil­ne’s beloved Win­nie the Pooh books.
Cre­at­ed between 1969 and 1972, Khitruk’s three films star a bear named “Vin­ni-Pukh” who looks noth­ing like the Win­nie the Pooh that West­ern­ers grew up with. (You can see the orig­i­nal illus­tra­tions of Pooh by E.H. Shep­ard here.) But view­ers will cer­tain­ly rec­og­nize the sto­ry­line and spir­it of the orig­i­nal Pooh in the Sovi­et adap­ta­tions. For decades, these films have enchant­ed East Euro­pean view­ers, both young and old. And they still occa­sion­al­ly appear on Russ­ian TV.
Above, you can watch the three ani­ma­tions online. They appear in the order in which they were released: 1) Win­nie-the-Pooh (Винни-Пух, 1969), 2) Win­nie-the-Pooh Goes on a Vis­it (Винни-Пух идет в гости, 1971); and 3) Win­nie-the-Pooh and the Day of Con­cern (Винни-Пух и день забот, 1972).

title: The San Francisco Public Library Launches a Free Online Archive with 80,000+ Historical Images & Documents to Explore & Download
description:
in Archives, History, Libraries |   	November 3rd, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			
Over 100,000 peo­ple move to the San Fran­cis­co Bay Area each year.
body:
in Archives, History, Libraries |   	November 3rd, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			
Over 100,000 peo­ple move to the San Fran­cis­co Bay Area each year. Their moti­va­tions for doing so no doubt vary, but these days, the ambi­tion to make a for­tune at the epi­cen­ter of the tech indus­try — espe­cial­ly amid the rapid­ly inflat­ing AI bub­ble — is hard­ly unheard of. Unfor­tu­nate­ly, that desire can be so all-con­sum­ing as to crowd out any inter­est in, or even curios­i­ty about, the city itself, to say noth­ing of its wider region. Yet the San Fran­cis­co we know today is the result of a sto­ry at least 250 years long, very lit­tle of which has much to do with ven­ture cap­i­tal or GPUs. Now, any­one who does want to make a start on under­stand­ing it can do so at the new-and-improved plat­form Dig­i­talSF, with its more than 80,000 his­tor­i­cal items avail­able to view and down­load.

An oper­a­tion of the San Fran­cis­co Pub­lic Library, Dig­i­talSF offers simul­ta­ne­ous access to mul­ti­ple online his­tor­i­cal archives. Search for the Gold­en Gate Bridge, let’s say, and the results will include hun­dreds of post­card pho­tographs and oth­er images cap­tur­ing that icon­ic piece of infra­struc­ture from a vari­ety of angles and in a vari­ety of decades, as well as — since this is the always cli­mat­i­cal­ly sur­pris­ing San Fran­cis­co we’re talk­ing about — under a vari­ety of weath­er con­di­tions.
The same exer­cise would prove equal­ly illu­mi­nat­ing for Chi­na­town, Pier 39, the Sutro Baths (which weren’t always ruins), and the Fer­ry Build­ing (which was­n’t always a col­lec­tion of pricey shops). Inevitably, this sort of vir­tu­al tourism becomes a form of time trav­el.

Dig­i­talSF also offers count­less glimpses of San Fran­cis­co’s impor­tant peri­ods in twen­ti­eth-cen­tu­ry Amer­i­can coun­ter­cul­ture, when the city made every­thing seem pos­si­ble: beat­nik poet­ry, the Grate­ful Dead, a par­tic­u­lar fla­vor of punk, the ascent of Har­vey Milk. But even before then, San Fran­cis­co had already expe­ri­enced a dis­pro­por­tion­ate­ly intense amount of his­to­ry dur­ing its rel­a­tive­ly short exis­tence: the earth­quakes of 1868 and 1906, for exam­ple, or the Gold Rush of the late eigh­teen-for­ties from whose par­tic­i­pants the local foot­ball team took its name. Those “forty-nin­ers” who flood­ed in from all over the rest of the Unit­ed States, turn­ing San Fran­cis­co from a small port town into a rel­a­tive­ly major city prac­ti­cal­ly overnight, prob­a­bly had scant fas­ci­na­tion with local his­to­ry them­selves. After all, they were too busy mak­ing it. Enter the Dig­i­talSF here.

Relat­ed con­tent:
An Archive of 5,000 Images Doc­u­ment the His­to­ry of San Fran­cis­co and the Vehi­cles That Put It in Motion
Dra­mat­ic Footage of San Fran­cis­co Right Before & After the Mas­sive­ly Dev­as­tat­ing Earth­quake of 1906
How the Gold­en Gate Bridge Was Built: A 3D Ani­mat­ed Intro­duc­tion
Rare Footage of the “Human Be-In,” the Land­mark Counter-Cul­ture Event Held in Gold­en Gate Park, 1967
The Unseen Sea: San Fran­cis­co Nat­ur­al Beau­ty in HD
Lawrence Fer­linghet­ti Turns 100: Hear the Great San Fran­cis­co Poet Read “Trump’s Tro­jan Horse,” “Pity the Nation” & Many Oth­er Poems
Based in Seoul, Col­in Marshall writes and broad­casts on cities, lan­guage, and cul­ture. He’s the author of the newslet­ter Books on Cities as well as the books 한국 요약 금지 (No Sum­ma­riz­ing Korea) and Kore­an Newtro. Fol­low him on the social net­work for­mer­ly known as Twit­ter at @colinmarshall.

title: A Beginner’s Guide to Philosophy: From Logic to Epistemology to Metaphysics
description:
in Photography |   	November 2nd, 2026  1 Comment
	
			

	

These are, per­haps, not the very best times for human­i­ties majors. Sel­dom do we even
body:
in Photography |   	November 2nd, 2026  1 Comment
	
			

	

These are, per­haps, not the very best times for human­i­ties majors. Sel­dom do we even hear the once-stan­dard defense that, by pur­su­ing a course of study in sub­jects of that kind, stu­dents “learn how to think.” Such a jus­ti­fi­ca­tion still points to real val­ue, at least in the most demand­ing set­tings. Take Har­vard’s course Human­i­ties 10, whose dig­i­tal device-free envi­ron­ment and syl­labus cov­er­ing every­thing from The Odyssey and Ulysses to Pla­to and James Bald­win — at a pace of one sub­stan­tial book per week — recent­ly drew the atten­tion of the Wall Street Jour­nal. Yet it’s always been true that you don’t have to major in any­thing to learn how to think, or in any case, to make a start of doing so.
Take the phi­los­o­phy-and-lit­er­a­ture YouTu­ber Jared Hen­der­son, who in the video at the top of the post tells us how he began his self-direct­ed study in high school. “I did what a lot of peo­ple would think is nat­ur­al,” he says. “I went to a book­store, and then I just found some books that I want­ed to read.” The pieces of light read­ing he took home: Friedrich Niet­zsche’s The Birth of Tragedy and Mar­tin Hei­deg­ger’s Intro­duc­tion to Meta­physics.
“If you know any­thing about phi­los­o­phy, I think you know that that was prob­a­bly not the ide­al way to start.” But all the years of learn­ing and teach­ing since have final­ly put him in a posi­tion of know­ing how to begin, and in the span of half an hour, he lays out an intel­lec­tu­al roadmap for any­one in the same posi­tion as his teenage self, with stops in log­ic, meta­physics, epis­te­mol­o­gy, ethics, and polit­i­cal phi­los­o­phy.
That sequence reflects the rea­son­able assump­tion that, before we can eval­u­ate argu­ments about how soci­ety ought to be arranged, we must learn to eval­u­ate state­ments about how things are. We must, in oth­er words, learn how to think — but also learn about the nature of real­i­ty itself, and how or whether we can know any­thing about it in the first place, ques­tions rel­e­vant to both meta­physics and epis­te­mol­o­gy. That may seem like a daunt­ing task, but Hen­der­son frames all its stages in rela­tion to one anoth­er, nam­ing some of the most famous philoso­phers who have writ­ten in the rel­e­vant fields along the way. No sin­gle read­ing could give you mas­tery of their work, or even a full under­stand­ing of it, how­ev­er clear the big­ger pic­ture might seem. But the attempt teach­es the true first les­son of phi­los­o­phy: in one area of knowl­edge or anoth­er, you’ll always be a begin­ner.
Relat­ed con­tent:
Free Online Phi­los­o­phy Cours­es

title: Watch David Bowie Take MTV to Task for Failing to Play Music Videos by Black Artists (1983)
description: The old vaude­ville phrase “Will it play in Peo­ria?” has its roots in the late 19th cen­tu­ry, specif­i­cal­ly in Hor­a­tio Alger’s nov­el F
body:
The old vaude­ville phrase “Will it play in Peo­ria?” has its roots in the late 19th cen­tu­ry, specif­i­cal­ly in Hor­a­tio Alger’s nov­el Five Hun­dred Dol­lars; Or Jacob Marlowe’s Secret. Like all of the books Alger wrote extolling the virtues of thrift, study, groom­ing, indus­try, etc., this one artic­u­lates a mid­dle Amer­i­can boot­straps phi­los­o­phy and rags-to-rich­es mythol­o­gy, while giv­ing the enter­tain­ment indus­try a col­or­ful way to sum up the small-town audi­ences who embraced Alger’s strait-laced eth­ic, and who need­ed to be pan­dered to or they wouldn’t get all those big-city jokes and ref­er­ences.
Peo­ria has been many places in the U.S.—from Tul­sa to Boise—but what­ev­er the test mar­ket, the assump­tions have always been the same: the Amer­i­can main­stream is insu­lar, mid­dle class or aspir­ing to it, cul­tur­al­ly con­ser­v­a­tive, unfail­ing­ly white, and fear­ful of every­one who isn’t. Such demo­graph­ic dog­ma has per­sist­ed for over a hun­dred years. Even when it is shown to be out­mod­ed or plain wrong, broad­cast­ers and jour­nal­ists con­tin­ue to play to Peo­ria, gen­u­flect­ing to a sta­t­ic, pop­ulist ver­sion of the U.S. that ignores large, rapid­ly chang­ing seg­ments of the pop­u­la­tion.
In the ear­ly eight­ies it took an Eng­lish­man with a very high pro­file to inter­ro­gate this state of affairs on the air. You may have come across the inter­view after David Bowie died, when social media filled with trib­utes and remem­brances. One thread that got a lot of atten­tion involved the tran­script of a 1983 inter­view Bowie gave the fledg­ling MTV, in which he “turns the tables on reporter Mark Good­man,” writes Takepart’s Jen­nifer Swann, “to grill him about the youth-ori­ent­ed network’s lack of eth­nic diver­si­ty.”
“It’s a sol­id enter­prise, and it’s got a lot going for it,” says Bowie. “I’m just floored by the fact there’s so few black artists fea­tured in it. Why is that?” On the spot, Good­man reach­es for a mar­ket­ing term, “nar­row­cast­ing,” to sug­gest that the net­work is delib­er­ate­ly tar­get­ing a niche. But when Bowie keeps push­ing, Good­man admits that the “nar­row” demo­graph­ic is the very same sup­posed mass mar­ket that exist­ed in Alger’s day, when the only rep­re­sen­ta­tions of black enter­tain­ers most white audi­ences in Peo­ria (or wher­ev­er) saw were in black­face.
We have to try and do what we think not only New York and Los Ange­les will appre­ci­ate, but also Pough­keep­sie or the Mid­west. Pick some town in the Mid­west that would be scared to death by Prince, which we’re play­ing, or a string of oth­er black faces, or black music. We have to play music we think an entire coun­try is going to like, and cer­tain­ly we’re a rock and roll sta­tion.
What do the Isley Broth­ers, asks Good­man, mean to a sev­en­teen-year-old? To which Bowie replies, “I’ll tell you what the Isley Broth­ers mean to a black sev­en­teen-year-old, and sure­ly he’s part of Amer­i­ca as well.” To the defense that it’s just the way things are, espe­cial­ly in radio, he gives a reply that might be derid­ed by many in the ready-made terms that rou­tine­ly pop up in such dis­cus­sions these days. Bowie, who suc­cess­ful­ly crossed over into play­ing for black audi­ences on Soul Train in the mid-sev­en­ties, would have sneered at phras­es like “SJW.” As he says in response to one young fan who rant­ed in a let­ter about “what he did­n’t want to see” on MTV: “Well that’s his prob­lem.”


	

The Peo­ria effect, says Bowie, “does seem to be ram­pant through Amer­i­can media. Should it not be a chal­lenge to make the media far more inte­grat­ed, espe­cial­ly, if any­thing, in musi­cal terms?” The “lines are begin­ning to blur,” Good­man admits. At the end of that year, Michael Jackson’s John Lan­dis-direct­ed “Thriller” video debuted and “changed music videos for­ev­er,” break­ing the prime­time bar­ri­ers for black artists on MTV, trans­form­ing the net­work “into a cul­tur­al behe­moth,” as Swann writes, and giv­ing the lie to the Peo­ria myth, one Bowie knew had lit­tle to do in actu­al­i­ty with the country’s cul­ture or its tastes but with a nar­row, archa­ic view of who the media should serve.
See Good­man’s full inter­view with Bowie just above.
Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2018.
Relat­ed Con­tent:

Josh Jones is a writer and musi­cian based in Durham, NC.

title: Jeffrey Gibson's 'A Real Love Thing' Surveys a Decade of the Artist's Multidisciplinary Practice
description: Through abstract, prismatic acrylic paintings to garment-like sculptures and textile collages, Jeffrey Gibson explores questions of identity, line
body:
Through abstract, prismatic acrylic paintings to garment-like sculptures and textile collages, Jeffrey Gibson explores questions of identity, lineage, and cultural translation. Working across media, the artist intricately beads monumental works and incorporates a wide range of fabrics and materials.
Jeffrey Gibson: A Real Love Thing at Johns Hopkins University Bloomberg Center delves into the cross-disciplinary breadth of the artist’s practice throughout the past decade. Fifteen works amplify his interest in pattern, queer iconography, and his Indigenous Mississippi Choctaw and Cherokee heritage. Drawing on the early and continuing influence of music, the artist often integrates song lyrics into tapestry-like wall hangings and three-dimensional works.
“Dewdrops in the Garden” (2025), acrylic on canvas, glass beads, artificial sinew, inset to custom wood frame, 70 x 80 inches. Courtesy of the artist and Hauser & Wirth
Music also inspired the title of the exhibition, which Gibson drew from a 1971 interview with soul artist Marvin Gaye, who described his seminal album What’s Going On by saying, “I think I’ve got a real love thing going. I love people, I love life, and I love nature, and I can’t see why other people can’t be like that.”
Reflecting this sentiment, Gibson’s approach is a luminous celebration of Indigenous symbolism and traditional materials, such as jingle cones used in ceremonial garments, tipi poles, and glass beads that have coated bags, moccasins, and other apparel hand-crafted by Native Americans throughout the centuries. The artist also posits a future full of hope, joy, acceptance, and, like Gaye, a love-above-all ethos.
A Real Love Thing continues through March 13 at the Bloomberg Center in Washington, D.C., where Gibson will present a talk as part of the esteemed Sam Gilliam Lecture series on November 12. And if you’re near Eugene, Oregon, the artist’s traveling solo exhibition They Teach Love is also on view through through March 7 at the University of Oregon.
Detail of “Dewdrops in the Garden.” Photo by Poll Bravo/Johns Hopkins University
Installation view of ‘Jeffrey Gibson: A Real Love Thing,’ Irene and Richard Frary Gallery, Johns Hopkins University Bloomberg Center, 2026. Photo by Poll Bravo/Johns Hopkins University
“Don’t Make Me Over” (2024), water-based ink on hand-dyed cotton fabric, canvas, polyester silk, polyester organza, acrylic felt, holographic vinyl, TPU laminated polyester fabric, glass beads, plastic beads, plastic sequins, artificial sinew, nylon thread, brass grommets and fabric weights, installed on pine tipi poles with hide, 79 x 88 x 18 inches. title: Faceted Faces and Surreal Still Lifes Fill GaHee Park's Dreamy Paintings
description: An eye peers from a goblet. A disembodied finger creeps from beneath a curtain. A supine figure, lost in a dream, envisions an uncanny array of ga
body:
An eye peers from a goblet. A disembodied finger creeps from beneath a curtain. A supine figure, lost in a dream, envisions an uncanny array of game and fruit. For GaHee Park, landscapes, figures, and still lifes merge into seamless, surreal tableaux. Her signature glassy-eyed female characters move through spaces where the boundary between reality and fantasy blurs.
Park’s new solo exhibition, Soft Shell at Jessica Silverman, delves into a realm where protection and a sense of security are nebulous. Although she nods to domestic spaces and symbols of comfort and sustenance, such as bowls laden with fruit, there is always something… else.
“Woman and Moth in Eclipse” (2026), oil on linen, 35 x 40 x 1 1/2 inches
At first glance, many of the scenes in Park’s oil paintings appear relaxed and calm, but something soon feels “off.” A dark cloud moves in above “Woman on the Beach with a Bird,” and an interloping digit advances toward a flower arrangement in “Bouquet with a Visitor.” Sometimes the strangeness is apparent right away, such as in “Soft Shell,” in which Park juxtaposes hard, distinct lines with supple, fuzzy shapes, and the whole scene appears to both expand and shrink.
The inspiration for this new body of work, along with the show’s title, is inspired by what the artist describes as “the containers of life that we inhabit to feel safe, but which do not protect us completely.” The artist explores the nature of consciousness and relationships between landscapes and interiors, beauty and the grotesque, and strength and vulnerability. Through a prism of dark humor, Park also infuses her works with subtle, quirky narratives.
In “Eating Angel,” for example, a white t-shirt and halo have been cast onto the floor, and a gleaming wing appears to have been picked clean by the curious cat. The nude female form, plus numerous anatomical hints in the shapes of fruit—or in this case, the breast-like cover on a food platter being presented from out of frame—Park also nods to the Surrealists. She turns the table on the early 20th-century works made predominantly by men, positioning women in roles of empowerment and directness. “Refusing to be conquered, these heroines are sly exhibitionists who draw the viewer into a ‘ping pong’ of gazes,” the gallery says.
Soft Shell continues through December 19 in San Francisco. Keep up with updates on Park’s Instagram.

title: “The Man I Love” Wants Us to Do More Than Mourn
description:
Film Review
                Ira Sachs resists the attention economy, using objects and people to tell a moving story of 1980s Ne
body:
Film Review
                Ira Sachs resists the attention economy, using objects and people to tell a moving story of 1980s New York amid the HIV/AIDS crisis.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Film still of The Man I Love (2026), directed by Ira Sachs (all images courtesy Cinetic Media)
    
        
            In a scene that might be this century’s most faithful depiction of 1980s bohemian New York, a ragtag ensemble crowds around a cluttered dining room table. A mishmash of stemware gleams below the revelers, each importuned to perform a few bars of a song. One self-consciously croons “Someone’s in the Kitchen with Dinah,” another vibratos a Jehovah’s Witness spiritual, while yet another gamely stumbles through the verses of “How Are Things in Glocca Morra?” from Finian’s Rainbow (1968). As gloriously languid as it is insistently idiosyncratic, the tableau readily summons nostalgia for those who remember and those who do not alike. There are no screens; there are no smartphones. There are instead people singing — shyly, joyfully — as though sharing the secret to the universe.And they are singing, knowing full well that some in the room might not last the year.A cinematic elegy that urges you to live, Ira Sachs’s The Man I Love is an AIDS movie that isn’t — a movie set in the thick of the pandemic that not only never mentions the illness by name, but entirely dodges the genre’s clichés: no lesion reveal, no tidy redemption, no funeral filled with festive friends. Instead, the film enjoins us to embrace the vitality of the era so as to more potently suffer its imminent loss.Film still of The Man I Love (2026), directed by Ira SachsThe Man I Love follows “theatre artist” Jimmy George (Rami Malek), a veteran of a downtown performance troupe, as he co-writes a new production and becomes enamored of a young Englishman named Vincent (Luther Ford) who moves into the downstairs unit of their weathered prewar building. Jimmy’s partner Dennis (Tom Sturridge) tolerates the burgeoning affair, but is duly irked by Vincent’s awkward attempts to ingratiate himself into their extensive queer network.
